Chapter Two: The Unreliability of Fortune and the Search for Lasting Happiness.
As time goes by, you might find your mind drifting back over everything that’s led you to this moment of loss. Isn’t it tempting to blame luck? Sometimes, life just feels like a roll of the dice—some people win, others lose, and it doesn’t always make sense. The idea of fortune, this mysterious force that seems to lift some folks up while knocking others down... it can be oddly comforting, but also a little cruel. It gives us a way to explain why suffering feels so random, but the downside is, it leaves us feeling powerless.
But then, wisdom steps in and asks—what actually is fortune? Is it really something that controls our lives, or is it just the name we give to life’s unpredictable ups and downs? Think about it: when things are going our way, we thank our lucky stars. When things fall apart, we blame bad luck. In both cases, we hand over our power, letting whatever happens outside of us decide how we feel about ourselves.
I remember a family who’d spent years just scraping by. Then, finally, they found some financial security. For a little while, life felt safe. But in a heartbeat, a sudden downturn wiped out their savings, and everything felt uncertain again. In the middle of all that anxiety, they realized something huge—their happiness had always depended on things they couldn’t control. The comfort they felt? It was never really theirs. It belonged to the ever-changing winds of fortune.
Wisdom offers us another way to look at happiness. Instead of chasing after things that can vanish—money, status, applause—it nudges us to look inward. Real happiness, it says, isn’t about what’s happening outside, but about the quality of your character and the strength of your mind. And this isn’t just wishful thinking—it’s actually practical. If your happiness depends on things that can be taken away, it’ll always feel shaky. But if it’s rooted in something inside you, it can last, even if everything else falls apart.
Most people push back against this at first. Wanting security is only natural. We all want to believe that if we just work hard enough, life will stay safe. But the truth is, no amount of planning can guarantee a future without loss. Think about all the stories you’ve heard of people who seemed to have it all, only to lose everything in a flash. The real lesson isn’t that happiness is out of reach—it’s that we need to look for it in a new place.
Wisdom tells another story—this time about someone who lost everything, yet somehow discovered a deep sense of peace that had nothing to do with what they owned or what they’d achieved. It’s not that they stopped caring about their losses; it’s that they realized their worth didn’t depend on them. They found comfort in the simple truth that while fortune can take away possessions and status, it can’t touch who you are at your core.
Of course, this kind of realization doesn’t come easy. It means letting go of old beliefs and sitting with the discomfort of not knowing what comes next. But as time goes on, it becomes clearer that chasing happiness outside ourselves is a race with no finish line. There’s always something else to want, always another fear waiting around the corner. True happiness, wisdom insists, comes from building up the habits of mind and heart—virtues that stay steady no matter what life throws at you.
